Sutherland
SUTH-ur-lund
n. (the northern Scottish county whose Strathnaver clearances of 1814 and after drove out its people, with some of its ministers preaching the evictions as providence)
Old Norse Suþrland, the south land, so named from the viewpoint of the Norse earls of Orkney and Caithness to the north.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sutherland is the great northern county of mountain and moor west of Caithness, and its name records that the Norsemen reckoned it their southern territory. Its history in the nineteenth century is the most notorious of the Highland clearances. The Sutherland estate, held by the Countess Elizabeth and her husband the Marquess of Stafford, covered most of the county, and between 1807 and 1821 its factors removed something like five thousand people from the inland straths, Strathnaver, Kildonan and Assynt among them, to coastal lots where they were to take up fishing, and turned the interior over to sheep. In 1814, the year the people called the year of the burnings, Patrick Sellar cleared Strathnaver; houses were fired, in some cases over the heads of the sick and aged, and an old woman died after being carried out of a burning cottage. Sellar was tried for culpable homicide in 1816 and acquitted by a jury of proprietors. Donald Macleod, a stonemason of Rossal, published his account as Gloomy Memories. The dictionary records the clearances, and names the part some ministers took in them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to evict as to dispossess by law; a factor as an agent; a strath as a valley; hire as wages; and an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor.

expand to see more

EVICT, v.t. To dispossess by a judicial process; to turn out of lands or tenements by law.

FACTOR, n. An agent employed by merchants or proprietors to manage their affairs and transact business.

STRATH, n. A valley of considerable size, through which a river runs; a term used in Scotland.

HIRE, n. The price, reward or compensation paid for the use of anything, or for personal service.

INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a permanent possession.

1Ki 21:3 — "And Naboth said to Ahab, The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee."

Eze 34:2 — "Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?"

Mic 3:11 — "The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us."

Psa 94:20 — "Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?"

Modern Corruption

Northern Scottish county where the Sutherland estate removed some five thousand people from the inland straths between 1807 and 1821, Strathnaver being burned in 1814 and Patrick Sellar acquitted of culpable homicide in 1816.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the clearance itself, and the dictionary names it as theft and in places as manslaughter. The tenants of Strathnaver held their ground by a possession older than the written titles of the family that evicted them, and they were put off it so that sheep might be run at a better rent. Naboth's answer is the answer of every such tenant and Scripture puts it in his mouth with approval: “The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee” (1Ki 21:3). Ahab got the vineyard by a legal process with witnesses, and a jury of proprietors acquitting a factor in 1816 is the same transaction; the psalmist has the name for it: “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20).

The second paragraph names the part the dictionary is most bound to name, because it was the church's. A number of the parish ministers of the Sutherland estate, presented by its patron and dependent on its goodwill, told their people from the pulpit that the removals were the will of God, that resistance was sin, and in some cases read the eviction notices themselves; others were silent. Ezekiel's indictment was written for shepherds in exactly that position: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2). Micah describes the arrangement that produces such preaching, where “The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire” (Mic 3:11), and notes that the men doing it still claimed the LORD was among them. The dictionary records that the people of these straths largely left the established church at the Disruption of 1843, and that they had been given every reason to.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Hebrew ra'ah (H7462), to shepherd; Hebrew 'amal (H5999), mischief.

expand to see more

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritage; “the inheritance of my fathers”, 1 Kings 21:3.

Hebrew chalilah (H2486) — far be it, God forbid; “The LORD forbid it me”, 1 Kings 21:3.

Hebrew ra'ah (H7462) — to pasture, to tend, to shepherd; “should not the shepherds feed the flocks?”, Ezekiel 34:2.

Hebrew mechir-sense of hire in Micah's charge — “the priests thereof teach for hire”, Micah 3:11.

Hebrew 'amal (H5999) — toil, trouble, mischief; “which frameth mischief by a law”, Psalm 94:20.

Usage

"“the inheritance of my fathers” (1Ki 21:3) — Strathnaver cleared in 1814."

"“should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2) — ministers reading the eviction notices."

"“which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20) — a jury of proprietors, 1816."
